\chapter{Eye, Ear, Mouth, and Nose}
\label{ch:mr-face-parts}
\hlchaptermodality{12}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the eye, ear, mouth, and nose in Marathi, say the retroflex \mr{ळ} formally for the first time, and tell which of the four carries the most secure English cognate and which replaced its own inherited word entirely.}

The chapter closes on \mr{नाक}, completing the face: the reader produces \mr{डोळा}, \mr{कान}, \mr{तोंड} and \mr{नाक} with their genders, and sorts the four by kind of history — \mr{डोळा} replaced the old Indo-Aryan eye-word with one that once meant \textquotedblleft{}swing\textquotedblright{}; \mr{कान}'s root is honestly disputed; \mr{तोंड} keeps a formal doublet, \mr{मुख}, standing beside it; \mr{नाक} alone reaches English \mr{नोज़} / nose without qualification.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ḍoḷā]{\mr{डोळा} (ḍoḷā) — the letter you've heard since Chapter 4, formally}

\label{lesson:MR-C12-dola}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मित्र}, \mr{कुटुंब}, \mr{भाऊ}, \mr{बहीण}} (\emph{mitra, kuṭumb, bhāū, bahīṇ}) — the people you'd introduce. This chapter turns to the body you'd ask after when you check how someone is.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{डोळा}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{डोळा}} — \emph{ḍoḷā} — \textbf{eye} (masculine)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\mr{ड}} you have from \emph{āvaḍṇe}; \textbf{\mr{ो}} the familiar \emph{o} mark, from \emph{bolṇe}. Then \textbf{\mr{ळ}} — the \textbf{retroflex \textquotedblleft{}l\textquotedblright{}} you first met, unlabeled, inside Chapter 4's \textbf{\mr{काळजी}}. Formally: tongue curled back, same place as \textbf{\mr{ट}} and \textbf{\mr{ण}}. Standard Hindi dropped this sound centuries ago; Marathi kept it, sharing it with the Dravidian languages to the south and with Gujarati. \emph{Ḍo-ḷā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{डोळा}} continues Maharastri Prakrit \textbf{ḍola}, \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{दोल}} \emph{dola} — \textquotedblleft{}a swing, a swinging.\textquotedblright{} Somewhere in Prakrit, \textquotedblleft{}a swinging thing\textquotedblright{} came to mean \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} and that word pushed out the one you might expect: the true inherited Indo-Aryan eye-word is Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{अक्षि}}/\textbf{\mr{अक्ष}} \emph{akṣi/akṣa}, from Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*h\textsubscript{3}ek\textsuperscript{w}-}}, the very cousin of Latin \textbf{oculus} and English \textbf{eye}. Hindi's \textbf{\mr{आँख}} \emph{ā̃kh} continues that old word, worn down through Prakrit \emph{acchi}. Marathi's eye is not that word at all — it is a replacement, built on something that once just meant \emph{swing}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{ḍoḷā} — eye
  \item \emph{Say it:} what its Sanskrit root actually meant — \textquotedblleft{}a swing\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Name:} the word Marathi's eye-word replaced — \textbf{akṣi}, Hindi's \textbf{āṅkh}
  \item \emph{Say it:} what you do with your \textbf{\mr{डोळे}} — \textbf{pāhṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to see,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 7's verb whose own root was Indo-European \emph{*spek-}
  \item \emph{Recall:} Chapter 11's tatsama/tadbhava split — \textbf{\mr{मित्र}, \mr{कुटुंब}} taken up whole, \textbf{\mr{भाऊ}, \mr{बहीण}} worn down — and \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}}'s own neuter gender against Hindi's masculine
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \textbf{\mr{डोळा}}'s Sanskrit root originally mean? (\textbf{A swing}.) Is \textbf{\mr{डोळा}} the same word as Hindi's \textbf{\mr{आँख}}? (\textbf{No} — Marathi replaced the old eye-word entirely.) What Marathi letter appears in \textbf{\mr{डोळा}} that Hindi lost? (\textbf{\mr{ळ}}, the retroflex \emph{l}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A1\%E0\%A5\%8B\%E0\%A4\%B3\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{डोळा}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A6\%E0\%A5\%8B\%E0\%A4\%B2}{Wiktionary: \mr{दोल}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kān]{\mr{कान} (kān) — an ear, and a cluster you've seen simplify before}

\label{lesson:MR-C12-kaan}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{डोळा}} (\emph{ḍoḷā}) — its own root turned out to be a surprise, a swing, not the old eye-word. This next word has a different kind of surprise: not what it meant, but how its middle got simpler.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{कान}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{कान}} — \emph{kān} — \textbf{ear} (masculine)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Nothing new. \textbf{\mr{क}}, \textbf{\mr{ा}}, \textbf{\mr{न}} are all familiar from Chapter 1 onward. \emph{Kā-n}.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\mr{कान}} continues Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{कर्ण}} \emph{karṇa}. Getting there took the same kind of step Chapter 6 traced in \textbf{\mr{दोन}}: Prakrit could not keep Sanskrit's consonant cluster \textbf{rṇ} intact, so it simplified — not by copying a neighbor this time, but by \textbf{doubling} the surviving consonant, \emph{rṇ} $\to$ \emph{ṇṇ}, giving Prakrit \textbf{\mr{कण्ण}} \emph{kaṇṇa}. Old Marathi then simplified the geminate back down to one \emph{ṇ} with a lengthened vowel: \emph{kāna}. Different cluster, different path, same underlying habit — Prakrit does not tolerate what Sanskrit could pack into one syllable.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
Past Sanskrit, \textbf{\mr{कर्ण}}'s own origin is genuinely \textbf{disputed} among scholars — proposals connect it to a word for \textquotedblleft{}point, spike,\textquotedblright{} to a root for \textquotedblleft{}handle, grip,\textquotedblright{} even to the verb \textquotedblleft{}to hear,\textquotedblright{} but none has won general acceptance. Rather than choose one and present it as settled, this lesson names the dispute and stops there, the same honest gap Chapter 11 named for \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}}, and the same restraint that kept \textbf{\mr{बहीण}} from being handed a false cousin — \textbf{\mr{बहीण}} looks like it should match English \emph{sister}, and does not.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{kān} — ear
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \emph{karṇa} $\to$ \emph{kaṇṇa} $\to$ \emph{kāna}, the cluster ground down and then simplified again
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{ḍoḷā, kān} — eye, ear
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Prakrit do to Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{कर्ण}}'s \emph{rṇ} cluster? (\textbf{Doubled it} to \emph{ṇṇ}, then Old Marathi simplified that back to one \emph{ṇ}.) Is \textbf{\mr{कर्ण}}'s root beyond Sanskrit settled? (\textbf{No} — disputed.) Which Chapter 6 word also showed a consonant cluster changing shape? (\textbf{\mr{दोन}}, whose final \emph{n} came from copying \textbf{\mr{तीन}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%A8}{Wiktionary: \mr{कान}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tõḍ]{\mr{तोंड} (tõḍ) — the mouth, and the formal word standing behind it}

\label{lesson:MR-C12-tond}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{डोळा}, \mr{कान}} — eye, ear. Recall how \textbf{\mr{कान}}'s middle got simpler — \emph{rṇ} doubled to \emph{ṇṇ}, then simplified again. One more word before the chapter's closing one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{तोंड}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{तोंड}} — \emph{tõḍ} — \textbf{mouth} (neuter)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Nothing new. \textbf{\mr{त}}, \textbf{\mr{ो}}, \textbf{\mr{ं}}, \textbf{\mr{ड}} are all familiar. \emph{Tõ-ḍ}, the anusvāra nasalizing the \emph{o}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{तोंड}} continues Maharastri Prakrit \textbf{\mr{तुंड}} \emph{tuṃḍa}, from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{तुण्ड}} \emph{tuṇḍa}, \textquotedblleft{}mouth, snout, beak\textquotedblright{} — a tadbhava, worn down the way \textbf{\mr{भाऊ}} was. Marathi keeps a second, formal word for the same thing: \textbf{\mr{मुख}} \emph{mukh}, borrowed whole from Sanskrit exactly the way \textbf{\mr{मित्र}} and \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}} were — the same everyday-versus-formal split \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}}'s chapter didn't need to show you for a body part until now. You'll hear \textbf{\mr{तोंड}} in daily speech and \textbf{\mr{मुख}} in writing, formal address, and words like \emph{mukhya}, \textquotedblleft{}chief, principal\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}at the mouth/face of things.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{tõḍ} — mouth
  \item \emph{Name:} its formal doublet — \textbf{mukh}
  \item \emph{Say it:} three so far — \textbf{ḍoḷā, kān, tõḍ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\mr{तोंड}}'s formal Sanskrit doublet? (\textbf{\mr{मुख}}, \emph{mukh}.) Is \textbf{\mr{तोंड}} itself borrowed whole or worn down? (\textbf{Worn down} — a tadbhava, like \textbf{\mr{भाऊ}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A4\%E0\%A5\%8B\%E0\%A4\%82\%E0\%A4\%A1}{Wiktionary: \mr{तोंड}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nāk]{\mr{नाक} (nāk) — the face, completed}

\label{lesson:MR-C12-naak}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{डोळा}, \mr{कान}, \mr{तोंड}} (\emph{ḍoḷā, kān, tõḍ}) — say them. One face part left, and it is the one with the plainest history of the four.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{नाक}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{नाक}} — \emph{nāk} — \textbf{nose} (neuter)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Nothing new. \textbf{\mr{न}}, \textbf{\mr{ा}}, \textbf{\mr{क}} — all familiar since Chapter 1. \emph{Nā-k}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{नाक}} continues Prakrit \textbf{\mr{णक्क}} \emph{ṇakka}, \textquotedblleft{}nose,\textquotedblright{} built on Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{नस्}} \emph{nas-}, \textquotedblleft{}nose,\textquotedblright{} plus a suffix. You may have met the \emph{other} Sanskrit route to \textquotedblleft{}nose,\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\mr{नासिका}} \emph{nāsikā}, elsewhere — Marathi's \textbf{\mr{नाक}} took the shorter one, straight from the bare root. Either way the destination is the same Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*neh\textsubscript{2}s-}}, which English inherited directly as \textbf{nose}. Of this chapter's four words, \textbf{\mr{नाक}} is the one whose English cousin needs no qualification at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Run the face back one more time, and notice each word told a different kind of story: \textbf{\mr{डोळा}} replaced its old Indo-Aryan word entirely, with something that once just meant \emph{swing}; \textbf{\mr{कान}}'s root is honestly \textbf{disputed}, even though its \emph{rṇ} $\to$ \emph{ṇṇ} $\to$ \emph{ṇ} path is not; \textbf{\mr{तोंड}} keeps a formal Sanskrit doublet, \textbf{\mr{मुख}}, standing beside it; and \textbf{\mr{नाक}} is the plainest of the four — a straight, secure line to Sanskrit and to English both. Not every word in a family carries the same amount of history, and knowing which is which is worth more than assuming they all match.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} all four, with gender — \textbf{ḍoḷā} m, \textbf{kān} m, \textbf{tõḍ} n, \textbf{nāk} n
  \item \emph{Name:} which is a secure English cousin (\textbf{nāk}), which replaced its old word (\textbf{ḍoḷā}), which is disputed (\textbf{kān}), which has a formal doublet (\textbf{tõḍ})
  \item \emph{Say it:} what you do with your \textbf{\mr{डोळे}} — \textbf{pāhṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which English word is \textbf{\mr{नाक}}'s most secure cousin? (\textbf{Nose}.) Sort the four face words by their history — replaced, disputed, twinned, secure. (\textbf{Ḍoḷā} replaced its old word; \textbf{kān}'s root is disputed; \textbf{tõḍ} has the formal doublet \textbf{mukh}; \textbf{nāk} is the secure one.) What Chapter 7 verb names what your eyes do? (\textbf{Pāhṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to see.\textquotedblright{})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A8\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%95}{Wiktionary: \mr{नाक}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
